questions.question: What are the main List implementations in Java and how do they differ?
questions.title: Java List Implementations: ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector
questions.direct_answer: **ArrayList** is a resizable array with O(1) random access. **LinkedList** is a doubly linked list with O(1) add/remove at head or tail but O(n) random access. **Vector** is a legacy synchronized ArrayList, generally replaced by ArrayList with external synchronization.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of List implementations and their time complexity trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying LinkedList is always faster for insertions — it's only faster for head/tail; middle insertion still requires O(n) traversal
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that LinkedList also implements Deque, making it useful as a queue or stack

sections.title: The Three List Implementations
sections.content:
**ArrayList** — backed by an `Object[]` array. When you call `get(i)`, it's a direct array index lookup: O(1). Adding to the end is amortized O(1) — occasionally the array doubles in capacity. Inserting in the middle is O(n) because elements must shift.

**LinkedList** — each element is a `Node` holding data, a `prev` pointer, and a `next` pointer. Adding to head or tail is O(1). Getting by index is O(n) because you traverse from the head. LinkedList also implements `Deque`, so it doubles as a queue or stack.

**Vector** — essentially ArrayList with `synchronized` on every method. Thread-safe but slow due to lock overhead. Modern code uses `ArrayList` with `Collections.synchronizedList()` or `CopyOnWriteArrayList` instead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- ArrayList: O(1) get, amortized O(1) add-end, O(n) add-middle or remove-middle
- LinkedList: O(1) add/remove at head or tail, O(n) get by index
- LinkedList implements Deque — usable as Queue or Stack
- Vector: legacy synchronized ArrayList — avoid in new code
- Default capacity: ArrayList starts at 10, doubles; LinkedList has no initial capacity

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Java has three main List implementations. ArrayList is backed by an array — get by index is O(1), adding to the end is amortized O(1), but inserting in the middle is O(n) because elements need to shift. LinkedList uses doubly linked nodes — add or remove at head or tail is O(1), but random access is O(n) since you traverse the chain. LinkedList also implements Deque so it works as a queue. Vector is a legacy thread-safe ArrayList that's been superseded — new code uses ArrayList with external synchronization instead.

questions.question: How does ArrayList resize internally when it runs out of capacity?
questions.title: ArrayList Internal Resizing Mechanism in Java
questions.direct_answer: When the backing array is full, ArrayList creates a new array at **1.5x the current capacity** (specifically `oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)`), copies all elements via `Arrays.copyOf`, and discards the old array. This is why add-to-end is amortized O(1), not always O(1).

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of ArrayList's internal array mechanics and amortized complexity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying ArrayList doubles capacity — it actually grows by 50% (1.5x), not 2x. Vector doubles.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that you can use new ArrayList<>(initialCapacity) to avoid resizes when you know the size upfront

sections.title: The Resize Process
sections.content:
ArrayList starts with a default capacity of **10** (or 0 if created with `new ArrayList<>()`). When you add the 11th element:

1. `ensureCapacity` detects the array is full
2. New capacity = `oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)` = 10 + 5 = **15**
3. `Arrays.copyOf(elementData, newCapacity)` copies all elements to the new array
4. The old array is garbage collected

```java
// Pre-size to avoid resizing if you know the count
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(1000);
```

This grow-by-50% strategy ensures that across N additions, the total copy work is O(N), making each add amortized O(1). Vector, by contrast, doubles its capacity (2x).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Default initial capacity: 10
- Growth factor: 1.5x (oldCap + oldCap/2)
- Vector growth factor: 2x (doubles)
- All existing elements are copied to the new array on resize
- Use `new ArrayList<>(n)` to pre-size when count is known
- `trimToSize()` shrinks the backing array to the current size

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: ArrayList starts with a default capacity of 10. When the backing array is full and you add another element, it creates a new array at 1.5 times the old capacity — so 10 becomes 15, 15 becomes 22, and so on — then copies everything over. This copy is O(n), but it happens infrequently enough that the amortized cost per add is still O(1). If you know upfront how many elements you'll add, you can pass an initial capacity to the constructor to avoid these resizes entirely.

beats.text: When an ArrayList's backing array is full, it creates a new array at 1.5 times the current capacity using the formula oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1), then copies all existing elements with Arrays.copyOf, and lets the old array be garbage collected. Default starting capacity is 10, so first resize goes to 15, then 22, then 33, and so on.

The 1.5x growth strategy makes the amortized cost of adding elements O(1). Across N additions the total copy work is O(N) — each element is copied at most a constant number of times across all resizes. This is the mathematical reason add-to-end is amortized O(1) despite occasional O(n) copies.

items: Default capacity: 10. First resize → 15. Second → 22. And so on at 1.5x each time.
Resize trigger: adding an element when size equals current capacity.
Vector uses 2x growth — ArrayList's 1.5x wastes less memory per resize.
Pre-sizing: new ArrayList<>(n) sets initial capacity to n, skipping all resizes for up to n elements.

beats.text: non-obvious: in the product catalog app, loading 100,000 products into new ArrayList<>() triggers about 24 resize-and-copy cycles. Initializing with new ArrayList<>(100000) does zero copies for the load phase — a measurable startup time improvement for large datasets.

items: Don't say ArrayList doubles — that's Vector's behavior. ArrayList grows by 50% (1.5x) — a common interview misconception.
trimToSize() shrinks the backing array to exactly the current size — useful after a large batch load if memory is tight, but it disables the amortized benefit for future adds.

speakable_v2.cap: ArrayList grows at 1.5x (not 2x), resize is O(n) but amortized O(1) per add — and pre-sizing eliminates all resize overhead when size is known.

questions.question: What does it mean that LinkedList implements the Deque interface?
questions.title: LinkedList as Deque in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Deque** (Double-Ended Queue) allows adding and removing from both ends. Since LinkedList has head and tail pointers, all four operations — `addFirst`, `addLast`, `removeFirst`, `removeLast` — are O(1), making LinkedList a natural Deque and Queue implementation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows LinkedList's dual role as List and Deque
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that LinkedList can be used as a queue or stack — many freshers only know it as a List
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention ArrayDeque is usually preferred over LinkedList for pure Deque/queue usage — it has better cache performance

sections.title: LinkedList as a Deque
sections.content:
`LinkedList` implements both `List<E>` and `Deque<E>`. Deque (pronounced 'deck') is a Double-Ended Queue — you can efficiently add or remove from either end:

```java
Deque<String> deque = new LinkedList<>();
deque.addFirst("A");   // head insert O(1)
deque.addLast("B");    // tail insert O(1)
deque.removeFirst();   // head remove O(1)
deque.peekLast();      // tail peek O(1)
```

Used as a **Queue**: `offer(e)` adds to tail, `poll()` removes from head — FIFO.
Used as a **Stack**: `push(e)` adds to head, `pop()` removes from head — LIFO.

Note: `ArrayDeque` is generally preferred for pure queue/deque usage because it avoids per-node object overhead and has better CPU cache behavior.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- LinkedList implements both List and Deque
- Deque: add/remove at both ends O(1)
- Queue mode: offer (tail), poll (head) — FIFO
- Stack mode: push (head), pop (head) — LIFO
- ArrayDeque is preferred for pure Deque use — no per-node overhead
- LinkedList uses more memory due to node objects (prev + next pointers)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: LinkedList implements both List and Deque. Deque means Double-Ended Queue — you can add and remove from both the head and tail in O(1) time because LinkedList has direct pointers to both ends. This makes it usable as a queue by adding to the tail and removing from the head, or as a stack by pushing and popping from the head. That said, for pure queue or deque usage, ArrayDeque is usually preferred because it has no per-node object overhead and performs better due to array locality.

beats.text: LinkedList implements both List and Deque. Deque (pronounced 'deck') is a Double-Ended Queue — you can add and remove elements from both the head and the tail. LinkedList has direct first and last pointers, so all four end operations — addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast — are O(1). This makes it naturally suitable as a queue (FIFO) or a stack (LIFO).

LinkedList's node structure with prev and next pointers makes end operations trivially O(1). Adding Deque support was a natural extension. It lets you reuse one class as a List, a Queue, or a Stack depending on which API you program against.

items: Queue mode (FIFO): offer(e) adds to tail, poll() removes from head — classic task processing.
Stack mode (LIFO): push(e) adds to head, pop() removes from head — undo history, depth-first search.
Deque mode: addFirst / addLast / removeFirst / removeLast — all O(1) in any combination.
ArrayDeque alternative: same O(1) ends but backed by an array — better cache locality, often faster in practice.

beats.text: non-obvious: when you declare Deque queue = new LinkedList<>(), you're hiding the List interface entirely — your code only sees the queue operations. Switching to new ArrayDeque<>() later is then a one-line change with no refactoring, and you get better cache performance for free.

items: Don't use LinkedList when ArrayDeque would serve the same queue/stack purpose — ArrayDeque avoids per-node overhead and has better memory locality.
Don't mix List and Deque methods on the same LinkedList without care — offer/poll and add/remove are separate method families with different null-handling behavior.

speakable_v2.cap: LinkedList's Deque face is powerful — but for pure queue or stack work, ArrayDeque is the better default with no linked-node overhead.

questions.question: Why is Vector considered legacy and what replaced it?
questions.title: Why Vector Is Legacy in Java and What Replaced It
questions.direct_answer: **Vector** is synchronized on every method, which causes unnecessary lock overhead even in single-threaded code. Modern replacements are **ArrayList** (unsynchronized, wrap with `Collections.synchronizedList` if needed) or **CopyOnWriteArrayList** (for concurrent read-heavy scenarios).

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Java's evolution and thread-safety trade-offs in collections
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Vector is still a valid thread-safe option — it has coarse-grained synchronization that doesn't actually protect compound operations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Point out that even Vector's synchronization is insufficient for compound operations like check-then-act — you'd still need external synchronization

sections.title: The Problem with Vector
Key Points
sections.content:
- Vector: synchronized on every method; Java 1.0 legacy
- Problem: overhead in single-threaded code; compound ops still unsafe
- Replace with ArrayList for single-threaded use
- Use Collections.synchronizedList(list) for basic thread safety
- Use CopyOnWriteArrayList for concurrent read-heavy scenarios
- Stack (extends Vector) is also legacy — use ArrayDeque instead

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Vector is legacy because it synchronizes every single method, which adds lock overhead even when you're running on a single thread. Plus the synchronization is coarse-grained — compound operations like check-then-add are still not atomic. Modern code uses ArrayList for single-threaded work, Collections.synchronizedList if you need basic thread safety, or CopyOnWriteArrayList for concurrent scenarios with many reads and few writes. Stack, which extends Vector, is similarly legacy — ArrayDeque is the recommended replacement.

speakable_v2.hook: Vector locks every method on every call — even in single-threaded code — and it doesn't even make compound operations safe.

beats.text: Vector is a synchronized List from Java 1.0. Every method — add, get, remove, size — acquires the object's intrinsic lock on every call, even in single-threaded code. That's unnecessary overhead. Worse, the method-level synchronization doesn't protect compound operations like check-then-add, so it gives a false sense of thread safety.

Vector was the only resizable list when Java launched in 1995. Thread safety was baked in because the designers expected concurrent access everywhere. ArrayList arrived in Java 2 (1998) as an unsynchronized, faster alternative. Vector stayed for backward compatibility but has been superseded.

items: Problem 1: Lock overhead on every method call, even single-threaded — measurably slower than ArrayList.
Problem 2: Compound ops like if(!v.contains(x)) v.add(x) are still not atomic — a race condition exists between contains and add.
Modern replacement for single-threaded: ArrayList — no locking overhead.
Modern replacement for thread-safe: Collections.synchronizedList() for basic wrapping, CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-heavy concurrent lists.

beats.text: non-obvious: Stack extends Vector, so it's also legacy — every Stack operation acquires a lock. The modern replacement is ArrayDeque used as a stack with push/pop. In a product catalog app, using Stack for undo history is slower than necessary — ArrayDeque does the same thing without any locking overhead.

items: Don't recommend Vector for thread-safe List usage — ConcurrentHashMap and CopyOnWriteArrayList are the correct modern answers.
Don't forget that Stack extends Vector and carries the same legacy problems — always use ArrayDeque as a stack replacement.

speakable_v2.cap: Vector is legacy — use ArrayList for single-threaded code, CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-heavy concurrent scenarios, and ArrayDeque for stack operations.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of common ArrayList operations?
questions.title: ArrayList Time Complexity: get, add, remove, contains
questions.direct_answer: `get(i)` is **O(1)** (direct array index). `add(e)` to end is **amortized O(1)**. `add(i, e)` or `remove(i)` in the middle is **O(n)** due to element shifting. `contains(o)` is **O(n)** — linear scan.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise knowledge of ArrayList's performance characteristics
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying add is always O(1) — it's amortized O(1), occasionally O(n) during resize
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why add-to-middle is O(n): all elements after the insertion point must be shifted right by one position

sections.title: ArrayList Complexity Table
sections.content:
| Operation | Complexity | Reason |
|-----------|-----------|--------|
| `get(i)` | O(1) | Direct array index lookup |
| `add(e)` (end) | Amortized O(1) | Occasionally O(n) on resize |
| `add(i, e)` (middle) | O(n) | Shift elements right |
| `remove(i)` (middle) | O(n) | Shift elements left |
| `remove(Object o)` | O(n) | Scan + shift |
| `contains(o)` | O(n) | Linear scan |
| `size()` | O(1) | Stored field |
| `set(i, e)` | O(1) | Direct array write |

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- O(1): get, set, size, add-to-end (amortized)
- O(n): add-to-middle, remove, contains, indexOf
- Amortized means: most adds are O(1), rare resize is O(n), average across all adds is O(1)
- ArrayList is NOT suitable as a queue (add-front is O(n))
- For frequent middle insertions, LinkedList or a different structure is better

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: For ArrayList: get by index is O(1) because it's a direct array lookup. Adding to the end is amortized O(1) — usually instant, occasionally O(n) when the array needs to resize and copy. Adding or removing in the middle is O(n) because every element after that position has to shift. Contains is O(n) — it scans the array linearly. So ArrayList is excellent for random access and appending, but not great for frequent middle insertions or deletions.

beats.text: ArrayList's time complexity depends on which operation you're calling. Get and set by index are O(1) — direct array access. Adding to the end is amortized O(1). Middle inserts and removes are O(n) because of element shifting. Contains and indexOf scan the entire array — O(n). size() is O(1) as it's a stored field.

The O(n) costs for middle operations and contains are fundamental to the array-backed design. Arrays give constant-time index access but require shifting for insertions and sequential scanning for value search. That's the trade-off you accept when you pick ArrayList.

items: O(1): get(i), set(i, e), size() — all direct array operations.
Amortized O(1): add(e) at end — instant most times, O(n) on rare resize.
O(n): add(i, e) and remove(i) in middle — elements must shift.
O(n): contains(o) and indexOf(o) — linear scan through the array.

If you frequently check membership, switch to a HashSet for O(1) contains. Keeping both a List for ordering and a HashSet for fast membership is a common performance pattern.

items: Don't say add is always O(1) — it's amortized O(1). An occasional resize makes a single add O(n), though the average remains O(1).
Don't use ArrayList for frequent membership testing — HashSet's O(1) contains is far faster than ArrayList's O(n) scan.

questions.question: When should you choose LinkedList over ArrayList in Java?
questions.title: When to Use LinkedList vs ArrayList in Java
questions.direct_answer: Choose **LinkedList** when you frequently add or remove elements at the **head or tail** (O(1)), use it as a **Queue or Deque**, and access by index rarely. In most other cases — especially with random access — **ArrayList** is the better choice.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical decision-making ability between two common implementations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying LinkedList is better for all insertions — middle insertion in LinkedList is still O(n) for the traversal
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that ArrayList usually wins in practice due to CPU cache efficiency — array elements are contiguous in memory, linked nodes are scattered

sections.title: LinkedList vs ArrayList Decision Guide
sections.content:
| Use Case | Winner | Why |
|----------|--------|-----|
| Random access by index | ArrayList | O(1) vs O(n) |
| Add/remove at head/tail | LinkedList | O(1) vs O(n) |
| Add/remove in middle | LinkedList* | O(1) node relink; O(n) to find position |
| Queue / Deque usage | LinkedList | Natural Deque; or use ArrayDeque |
| Memory efficiency | ArrayList | No per-node prev/next overhead |
| Cache performance | ArrayList | Contiguous memory, CPU cache-friendly |
| General default | ArrayList | Faster in most real benchmarks |

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- ArrayList: random access O(1), cache-friendly, less memory
- LinkedList: head/tail O(1), implements Deque — good as queue/stack
- Middle insert in LinkedList: still O(n) to traverse to position
- In practice, ArrayList beats LinkedList in most benchmarks due to cache locality
- Use ArrayDeque instead of LinkedList for pure queue/deque — even better cache performance

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Choose LinkedList when you need frequent add or remove at the head or tail — those are O(1) operations. It's also natural when you need queue or deque behavior. But for most other scenarios, ArrayList wins because random access is O(1) and the array's contiguous memory layout is CPU cache-friendly. Even middle insertions in LinkedList require O(n) traversal to find the position before the O(1) node relink. In practice, ArrayList outperforms LinkedList in most real-world benchmarks.
